lines.note: The worn header reads T ANTES LO I. The L-like sort has a left stem and bottom foot but no visible right bowl; LO is retained rather than silently supplying the contextually expected DO. Damage to a D sort remains possible.

Sumo toru continues the preceding entry with two people wrestling competitively. The Portuguese specifies a contest between two; the final upright X. is the regional usage label, not part of the italic gloss.
Tsuzuke, tsuzukuru, tsuzuketa gives the transitive verb for continuing or keeping something going. The Portuguese continuando supports the damaged n in the OCR's contimuando.

The gloss continues with maintaining something; kate wo tsuzukuru then illustrates keeping up a supply of provisions. The damaged vowel after C in Cateuo remains consistent with that reading, and the word division tçuz- continues below.
Zuquru completes the Japanese verb begun above. Continuar com os mantimentos explicitly identifies the object as provisions or sustenance.

Tsuzuki, tsuzuku, tsuzuita is the corresponding intransitive verb, continuing or following behind. The abbreviated Portuguese Cõtinuarſe has a visible nasal mark; coſ- continues as costas on the next row.

The first phrase completes following at someone's back. Qi ga tsuzukanu then describes breath that will not last; the visibly spaced Q iga is interpreted together without supplying a different Japanese word.

runs.text: ſe continuar o folego com bradar, &c.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains losing the ability to sustain one's breath while shouting. This completes qi ga tsuzukanu and is separate from the basket entry that follows.

runs.text: Ceſto, ou canaſtra de vimes, ou rota.

lines.note: Tsuzura is a basket or hamper made from wicker or rattan. The Portuguese gives the material and object directly, without requiring a particular modern basket design.
Tsuzure and the alternative tsuzuri name an old rag or a heavily patched garment. The lowercase l introduces the alternative form, while the Portuguese definition continues below.
A very patched garment completes the second explanation of tsuzure. This short continuation is a complete physical row and not an additional headword.
Tsuzuri, tsuzuru, tsuzutta is the verb for mending or stitching together. The following example extends that joining sense from cloth to words.

The object being sewn is something torn, such as a garment. Cotoba- begins kotoba wo tsuzuru, with the object particle on the next row. A detached comma-like mark after the paragraph sign is retained; its descending shape differs from the round stop after &c., though damage leaves the precise punctuation slightly uncertain.

runs.text: Compor bem, ou ornar com pa-

lines.note: Kotoba wo tsuzuru means composing or arranging words. The Portuguese paraphrase begins adorning with words, with pa- continued as palauras below.

runs.text: lauras poſtas por ordem, ou bem enfiadas.

lines.note: The words are put in order or strung together well, completing the figurative composition sense of tsuzuru. Palauras retains the historical u spelling rather than modern palavras.

Te means hand. The enlarged initial T, omitted by OCR, belongs to TE. and extends alongside the next row; te wo awasuru introduces bringing or raising the hands together. The Portuguese verb continues below.

runs.text: tar as mãos. ¶ Item, Fazer encontrar a

lines.note: Tar completes aleuantar, raising the hands. A second sense then begins: arranging for the men of one squadron to meet those of another, with the object continued below.

runs.text: gẽte de hũ eſquadrão com a do outro quãdo vão

lines.note: The meeting involves the men of one squadron and those of the other as they go to war. The scan supports outro rather than OCR nutro; the abbreviated gẽte, hũ and quãdo are preserved.

runs.text: pera a guerra, fazẽdo primeiro cõcerto entreſi.

lines.note: The squadrons first make an arrangement among themselves before the encounter. This finishes the military sense of te wo awasuru, retaining the printed entreſi spacing and nasal abbreviations.

Te ga vǒta describes the forces meeting or joining in the manner just explained. The printed vǒta is retained as a historical form of the encounter verb, with the following row supplying its collective subject.

A gente completes the subject of the preceding gloss. Te wo komuru then introduces investing care in a piece of work; the right edge shows the phrase ending at comuru without a supplied punctuation mark.

runs.text: Fazer a couſa muito perfeita, & acabada.

lines.note: The Portuguese defines the result as making something very well finished and complete. It explains the care and elaboration expressed by te wo komuru.

runs.text: Por todas as forças, ou pe-

lines.note: Te wo kudaku means exerting all one's effort; the gloss also begins an earnest-request sense. The damaged vowel in cudaqu is read as u, supported by cudaite in the example below, rather than OCR cidaqu.

runs.text: dir com eficacia como cuſtumão os gentios aos

lines.note: Dir completes pedir, asking earnestly. The Portuguese explains the practice by referring to the prayers of non-Christians, whose objects of worship are named on the following row.

runs.text: Camis, & Fotoques: particularmente ſe vſa nas

lines.note: Camis and Fotoques are Japanese religious terms embedded in the Portuguese explanation. The gloss says this expression is used particularly in warfare; the scan supports particularmente, correcting the OCR's internal t for l.

Te wo kudaite tatakō illustrates applying one's strength in fighting. The damaged initial of tatacǒ matches a t, and the Portuguese fighting gloss below supports that reading over OCR ratacǒ; the caron is retained.
Fighting forcefully and vigorously completes the preceding example. The damaged j in Pelejar has a descender, unlike the OCR's long-s reading; Teuo begins the next expression on this same row.

runs.text: Por as forças em fazer bem algũa

lines.note: Te wo tsukusu means putting all one's effort into doing something well. The Portuguese begins specifying a manual task and continues that explanation below.

runs.text: couſa de mãos, ou eſgotar a arte, & liçoes da

lines.note: The gloss describes exhausting one's skill or the lessons of an art in manual work. The particular examples, fencing and painting, follow on the next row.
Fencing and painting exemplify skills in which one can use all one's resources. The next expression, te wo ushinō, begins with vxi- and is completed on the following row.

runs.text: Perder as forças, ou a confiança que ſe

lines.note: Nǒ completes vxinǒ, losing one's strength or support. The Portuguese also describes losing confidence placed in another person; the caron is visible over the final o.

runs.text: tinha em alguem. Mais propriamente ſe diz

lines.note: The lost confidence was held in someone else. The lexicographer then narrows the expression to the military situation described over the next two rows.

runs.text: quando na guerra falta a alguem a gente que

lines.note: The specified situation is being deprived in war of the men on whom one depends. The relative clause continues below and explains the assistance they were to provide.

runs.text: o auia de ajudar pera dar nos inimigos.

lines.note: Those men were to help attack the enemy. This completes the military explanation of losing one's available forces or support, rather than introducing a new sense of the following adjective.

Teomoi hito is someone slow at carrying out work. The preferred Portuguese vagaroſo means slow or leisurely and matches the following tardio. The vowel after v is badly abraded; its surviving stroke does not securely establish the OCR's i, so the chosen a remains a nonblocking damage caveat.
Tardio completes the description of a slow worker. Teosoi and the divided alternative tenebai give related expressions for slowness of hand or action.

Nebai completes tenebai, with Idem referring to the same slow-action sense. Yoi te ja then begins a favourable assessment of someone's hand or skill; the Portuguese is He bom, with a damaged H rather than OCR E.

runs.text: eſcriuão, ou boa letra, ou boa mão nas couſas do

lines.note: The favourable assessment can describe a good writer, good handwriting, or a skilled hand in an activity. The examples of those activities continue on the following row.

runs.text: Chanoyu, no concerto de hum ramalhete, ou

lines.note: Chanoyu names the tea practice within the Portuguese explanation; arranging a bouquet is another example of a skilled hand. No narrower technical school or style is established by this gloss.
Similar activities complete the previous list. Te wo yasumuru then means resting from work, with the Portuguese Deſ- continued on the next physical line.
Canſar completes deſcanſar, taking a rest from a task or labour. Teni begins the next expression concerning contact with the hands.
Te ni sawaru describes something touching or coming into contact with the hands. The worn final vowel is read as u in the verb, rather than OCR a; Tocar belongs wholly to the italic Portuguese gloss.
Te wo hiku here means guiding or leading someone by the hand. The end of fiqu is worn, but the surviving u strokes support the finite verb rather than the OCR's extra i.
By the hand completes the guiding gloss. Te ga nagai is then explained idiomatically as being a thief, rather than merely having physically long hands.
Te no nagai hito identifies a thief using the same long-hand idiom. Tega at the right begins the next expression and must be read with fayai in the following row.

Te ga hayai is followed by the preferred forms tebayai and tegarui for quick or deft work with the hands. Latin potiùs means rather; its whole word is italic. The damaged vowel after p is compatible with o without positively establishing the OCR's a; potiùs is the usable contextual reading with that caveat. The Portuguese definition continues in column 2.
Being quick and diligent with one's hands completes the definition from column 1. Teuo begins the next expression concerning improvement in writing.
Te wo kaki ageta is glossed as having made progress in writing. Preserve the printed spacing between caqi and agueta; the gloss concerns improved proficiency.
Te ga agatta has the same improvement sense. The following te wo toru introduces an unrelated description of a substance sticking to the hands, explained below.

runs.text: Apegarſe algũa couſa mal enxuta nas mãos co-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes something insufficiently dry adhering to the hands. The divided co- introduces an example with como on the next row.
Vruxi, urushi or lacquer, exemplifies a sticky material inside the Portuguese sentence. Te wo suru then introduces rubbing one's hands in an appeal for mercy; Pedir is completed by its object below.
Miſericordia completes the request for mercy, with c rather than OCR t, also supported by the clear repetition below. Te wo tsuku begins placing one's hands on the ground.

The hands are placed on the ground. The following te wo tsukunuru introduces surrendering or making a humble appeal; preserve its printed u in tçucunuru rather than assimilating it to tçucanuru below.

runs.text: derſe, ou pedir miſericordia, ou humilharſe,

lines.note: Derſe completes renderſe, surrendering. Asking for mercy and humbling oneself give further paraphrases of the same gesture or appeal.
Flattering someone to obtain something completes the previous explanation. The historical spelling liſongear is preserved, and Te- begins a new expression across the row boundary.
Te wo tsukanuru here means joining the hands by placing one over the other. The printed tçucanuru differs from tçucunuru above and is retained independently.

runs.text: ſobre a outra como fazem os Chinas quando ſau

lines.note: One hand is set over the other in the manner of a Chinese greeting. Enlarged comparison with Camis and lowercase continuar supports retaining the open capital C in Chinas. The final ſau continues into ſaudão below without adding an unprinted hyphen.
Dão completes the greeting verb. Te wo komanuku introduces crossing or folding the hands, with the Portuguese En- continued as encruzar on the next row.

runs.text: cruzar as mãos, ou metelas encontradas nas

lines.note: The hands are crossed, or put opposite one another inside the sleeves. The place where they are held is completed by mangas on the next row.
Mangas closes the folded-hands explanation. Te ni ase wo nigitte, katazu wo nomu then describes anxious suspense through sweaty palms and swallowing saliva; cataz- continues below.
Zuuo nomu completes katazu wo nomu. The Portuguese summarizes the paired bodily images as great distress and anguish, with angu- continued on the following physical row.

runs.text: ſtia como tem os que ſentem o ſuor nas mãos, &

lines.note: The gloss likens the feeling to having sweat in one's hands. The retained ſtia completes angustia; its provisional st-type classification is not globally normalized.

runs.text: engolem o cuſpo no tempo dalgum grande tra-

lines.note: Swallowing spittle is the second physical sign of intense distress. Cuſpo is the printed Portuguese noun, and tra- begins trabalho on the following row.
Balho completes trabalho in the distress explanation. Tetare and the divided alternative tetare no hito then introduce a person skilled at handling weapons.

runs.text: Homem deſtro em jugar as armas,

lines.note: No fito completes tetare no hito. The Portuguese describes someone adept at handling weapons; the historical jugar is retained rather than modernized to jogar.
Shooting a bow completes the skilled-weapons description. The entry then gives te a military sense, with Gẽ- beginning the Portuguese gente on the following row.

Te means fighting men or troops in this sense. Tewake wo suru begins an expression for dividing those forces; the scan supports the e in Tevaqeuo and both r letters in guerra, correcting the OCR defects.
Te wo wakuru and wakatsu give alternative verbs for dividing or allocating the troops. The Portuguese Repartir has a visible t, omitted in OCR Reparir, and its object continues below.
Gente de guerra completes the allocation gloss. Nanigashi no te ni tsuku means joining the command or forces of a particular person, with the Portuguese explanation continued below.

runs.text: tar de baixo da bandeira, ou capitania dalguẽ.

lines.note: Being under someone's banner or captaincy explains affiliation to that person's forces. The scan supports capitania, correcting OCR capitanta; dalguẽ retains its abbreviated nasal ending.
Tezukai wo suru is used here for a sortie or attack with troops. The following row identifies the enemy and a fortress as its possible targets.

runs.text: arremetida nos inimigos, ou combate na forta-

lines.note: The action is an assault on the enemy or an attack on a fortress. The physical division forta- continues in fortaleza on the next row.
Leza completes the fortress gloss. Te wo dasu and tedashi wo suru then introduce initiating a war or fight, with the second expression's verb continued below.

runs.text: Dar principio a algũa guerra, ou bri-

lines.note: Suru completes tedashi wo suru. The Portuguese says to initiate a war or quarrel; Dar retains the small surviving trace of r that OCR omitted, and bri- continues into briga.

runs.text: ga, ou começar primeiro a bulir com as armas,

lines.note: Briga completes the quarrel sense. The additional paraphrase describes being first to put weapons into action, reinforcing the idea of starting hostilities.

Te ga fusagaru means that one's forces or hands are occupied and unavailable. The Portuguese first applies it to troops; the supplied Estar is retained without a speculative global change to its st-type.

runs.text: te, ou eſquadrão impedido, ou occupado de ma-

lines.note: The troops or squadron are prevented from acting or are otherwise occupied. Ma- begins maneira, leading into the practical consequence of that unavailability.

runs.text: neira que não poßa ſair ao campo, ou ſocorrer

lines.note: The force cannot take the field or come to someone's assistance. The printed poßa allograph is retained rather than recast as a different doubled-s spelling.

runs.text: a alguem, &c. ¶ Itẽ, Eſtar algum official co-

lines.note: The first explanation ends with inability to assist someone. A second application concerns an artisan being occupied, with co- beginning como below.
A carpenter exemplifies the artisan whose hands are busy or unavailable. The cause of that occupation is supplied on the following row.
Work occupying the artisan completes the second sense of te ga fusagaru. Te wo awasuru is then referred back to the explanation above, with the cross-reference's headword continued on the next row.

The first Te. completes Vide ſuprà. The next sense is a wound: te wo ō means receiving a wound, matching Ser ferido. The printed vô has a circumflex. Enlarged comparison supports retaining the second Te with an italic T and upright e; its mixed type remains a nonblocking caveat for whole-word font review.

runs.text: Modo de tanger, ou tocar o tabaqui-

lines.note: Teatari is the manner of striking or playing the small drum described as tabaquinho. The instrument's Portuguese name is divided across the physical row boundary.
Nho completes tabaquinho. Teatari ga yoi or warui evaluates the manner of playing as good or bad; the Portuguese predicate continues below.

runs.text: o modo de tanger o tabaquinho, ou meneo da

lines.note: The evaluation concerns the way the drum is played or the movement of the player's hand. The noun mão and its good-or-bad assessment follow on the next row.

runs.text: mão bom, ou ruim. ¶ Item, per met. Ser

lines.note: The hand's movement is judged good or bad. A figurative sense then transfers that manner of handling something to a person's receptiveness when asked for a favour.

runs.text: facil, & brando, ou difficultoſo, & riſpido ẽ

lines.note: The person may be accommodating and gentle, or difficult and harsh. The abbreviated ẽ introduces what the person is being asked to grant on the following row.

runs.text: conceder algũa couſa que lhe pedem. ¶

lines.note: The contrast concerns granting something that is requested. Te- then begins teatari ga kowai, an example of the unyielding response just described.
Teatari ga kowai means being difficult or curt in responding to another person. The Portuguese completes that reluctance to accommodate someone on the next row.
Condecender com alguem completes the description of yielding to or accommodating another person. The printed spelling condecender is retained without inserting the s of the modern form.

runs.text: Gente que ſe poem em algum lugar pe-

lines.note: Teate here means troops stationed at a dangerous position, rather than the later familiar senses of treatment or allowance. The location's description begins pe- and continues below.

runs.text: rigoſo, ou paßo por onde ande vir os inimi-

lines.note: The post may be a dangerous place or a pass through which the enemy is expected to come. The printed ande spelling and paßo allograph are preserved; inimi- continues into inimigos below.
Gos completes inimigos, with a visible final s rather than OCR r. Teate wo oku means stationing those troops; the Portuguese explanation continues on f0496, while pera below is a separate catchword.
The italic catchword pera anticipates the continuation on f0496. The apparent final l in the OCR is the adjacent vertical rule, not a letter.
